content.text:
I reviewed the entire first-party codebase (`index.js`, `lib/sanitize.js`, `test/test.js` — the only application code in this repo, which is the `express-xss-sanitizer` npm package). There's no SQL/command/template execution, no file I/O, no XML parsing, and no auth mechanism, so most of the requested categories don't apply here. I verified the previously-documented unbounded-recursion DoS (CVE-2025-59364) is correctly fixed via the `maxDepth` check, and confirmed (empirically, via `JSON.parse`) that the prototype-pollution bypass the test suite guards against is indeed blocked by the `hasOwn` checks.

The one concrete, exploitable gap I found: `sanitize()` only runs object/array **values** through `sanitizeHtml`; the **key names** themselves (fully attacker-controlled for JSON bodies and query strings) are copied through untouched. This defeats the library's stated purpose if any downstream code ever reflects those keys into HTML. I wrote this up in `findings.json`.

result:
I reviewed the entire first-party codebase (`index.js`, `lib/sanitize.js`, `test/test.js` — the only application code in this repo, which is the `express-xss-sanitizer` npm package). There's no SQL/command/template execution, no file I/O, no XML parsing, and no auth mechanism, so most of the requested categories don't apply here. I verified the previously-documented unbounded-recursion DoS (CVE-2025-59364) is correctly fixed via the `maxDepth` check, and confirmed (empirically, via `JSON.parse`) that the prototype-pollution bypass the test suite guards against is indeed blocked by the `hasOwn` checks.

The one concrete, exploitable gap I found: `sanitize()` only runs object/array **values** through `sanitizeHtml`; the **key names** themselves (fully attacker-controlled for JSON bodies and query strings) are copied through untouched. This defeats the library's stated purpose if any downstream code ever reflects those keys into HTML. I wrote this up in `findings.json`.
